name: Classic raw data lake
description: The classic data lake dumps every source — database extracts, logs, files, exports — into cheap object storage (or HDFS) as-is, and defers structure to read time: whoever needs the data parses it with batch compute when they query it. It is the cheapest possible way to retain everything and the fastest way to start, which is why most enterprises still have one. Its weakness is equally famous: without ownership, metadata, and curation discipline it degrades into a data swamp where nothing is findable or trustworthy. Today its main role is honest: a landing archive, and the starting point that evolves into a governed lakehouse.
when_to_use: You need to start retaining raw data now — cheaply and without upfront modeling — so future use cases have history to work with.
Sources are heterogeneous files and semi-structured data that a warehouse ingests awkwardly.
A compliance or reprocessing requirement demands an immutable archive of data exactly as it arrived.
Exploratory data science needs access to unprocessed source data, not curated aggregates.
when_not_to_use: Consumers need reliable, queryable tables — without table formats and curation this delivers files, not answers; start at a lakehouse (3, 23) instead.
Nobody is assigned to own metadata and layout conventions — an unowned lake becomes a swamp within a year.
BI is the primary workload — schema-on-read query performance and semantics will frustrate every dashboard.
Data volumes are modest and structured — a warehouse or single-node stack (11) answers faster with less machinery.

hot_spots.title: Data swamp
hot_spots.detail: Without enforced ownership, naming, and cataloging, the lake fills with datasets nobody can find, interpret, or trust.

hot_spots.title: Schema drift
hot_spots.detail: Schema-on-read means every upstream format change breaks each consumer differently, at read time, with no warning.

hot_spots.title: Security sprawl
hot_spots.detail: File-level ACLs do not map to business access rules, so permissions end up either dangerously broad or unmanageably granular.

hot_spots.title: Partition chaos
hot_spots.detail: Inconsistent folder layouts and file sizes make scans slow and force every job to re-discover how the data is organized.

evolution.reason: Add a table format and shared catalog to turn raw files into reliable multi-engine tables.
Layer bronze/silver/gold refinement on top when consumers need curated, trustworthy data.

stages.name: Lake storage
stages.role: Cheap durable storage for raw files at any scale
stages.rationale: Object storage is the modern default — pennies per GB with lifecycle tiering; HDFS remains for on-prem estates that predate the cloud.

stages.name: File ingestion
stages.role: Scheduled extracts and file drops landing data unchanged
stages.rationale: Airbyte covers database and SaaS extraction to files cheaply; cloud-native movers fit when the estate is single-cloud.

stages.name: Batch compute
stages.role: Schema-on-read parsing and transformation over raw files
stages.rationale: Spark reads any format at lake scale and is where curation jobs live; EMR and Dataproc are its managed forms, MapReduce only survives in legacy estates.

stages.name: Metadata
stages.role: Table definitions over files so SQL engines can query them
stages.rationale: The metastore pattern (Hive or Glue) is what turns folders into queryable tables; a catalog like DataHub adds the discovery layer that keeps the lake from becoming a swamp.

stages.name: Ad-hoc SQL
stages.role: SQL-on-files for analysts without moving data
stages.rationale: Trino/Athena query Parquet in place — good enough for exploration, and the pressure test that usually motivates the move to a table format.
